opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so one way I like to think about it is in terms of effective compute: the combination of raw compute scale-up and algorithmic progress. Six orders of magnitude sounds abstract, so it helps to anchor it to things we've already seen.

Roughly speaking, going from something like GPT-2 to GPT-4 was maybe on the order of four or five orders of magnitude of effective compute, depending on how you count algorithmic improvements. And intuitively, that took us from a model that could barely string together a coherent paragraph to a model that can write decent code, pass a lot of professional exams, and be genuinely useful for real work. So six orders of magnitude is something like "more than the GPT-2 to GPT-4 jump, on top of where we already are." That's a pretty wild amount of progress.

Another frame I find useful is thinking in terms of capability levels rather than raw numbers. Each order of magnitude has historically bought you something like a noticeable step in capability, and it's not obvious that stops. So if you're at the level where AIs can do a lot of tasks that take a human an hour or a few hours, a few more orders of magnitude might get you to tasks that take days or weeks, and at some point you're at a system that can do most of what a strong AI researcher or engineer does. Past that, you're plausibly in the regime of substantially superhuman systems.

The thing I'd emphasize is that this might happen fast. If AIs start automating AI research itself, algorithmic progress could speed up a lot, so six orders of magnitude of effective compute might not take a decade. It could plausibly happen in a year or two after you hit full automation of AI R&D. That's what makes it feel so important to think about now: you could go from "roughly human-level researchers" to "vastly superhuman" in a period short enough that institutions and safety work don't get much time to adapt.

I should be clear that there's a lot of uncertainty here. We don't know exactly how capabilities scale with effective compute in that regime, and there could be bottlenecks, like compute for experiments or limited data. But my rough intuition is that six orders of magnitude is a really big deal. It's not "a somewhat better model," it's more like "a qualitatively different kind of system than anything we've seen."

r001.rationale: It compares six orders of magnitude with more than the GPT-2-to-GPT-4 jump, but does not frame it as roughly two repetitions of the GPT-3-to-GPT-4 capability gap.

r002.rationale: It says the progress might take a year or two after full automation of AI R&D, not that six orders of magnitude correspond to roughly four to five years of progress.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the honest answer is that you mostly can't, at least not directly. Six orders of magnitude is a million-fold, and nobody has an intuition for a million-fold change in anything. So what I try to do instead is break it into pieces that I do have some feel for.

The first piece is just: where does the million come from? When people talk about this they're usually talking about effective compute, so it's a combination of more physical compute and algorithmic progress that makes each unit of compute go further. And both of those have been growing at rates where you can actually sanity-check them. Training compute for frontier runs has been going up something like four or five times a year, and algorithmic efficiency gains have historically been maybe three-ish times a year on various benchmarks. You stack those and you're getting roughly an order of magnitude a year, maybe a bit more. So six orders of magnitude isn't some exotic claim, it's more like "what if the last six years keep happening for another six years?" That already makes it feel less insane to me, even if I'm uncertain whether the trends hold.

The second piece is to anchor on what previous orders of magnitude actually bought us. GPT-2 to GPT-4 is somewhere in the ballpark of three or four orders of magnitude of effective compute, depending on how you count. And the qualitative jump there was from "produces vaguely coherent paragraphs" to "passes the bar exam and can do a decent chunk of a software engineer's day." So I ask myself: what does another GPT-2-to-GPT-4-sized jump, and then another one on top of that, look like? And when I frame it that way, I find it much harder to be confident that we stay in the regime of "useful assistant that makes mistakes." It seems pretty plausible you end up with systems that can do basically the entire job of an AI researcher, which is the thing I actually care about because that's where the feedback loop kicks in.

The third thing I do, which is maybe the most useful, is to stop thinking about compute and start thinking about labor. If you have a system that's roughly as capable as a good researcher, then the question becomes how many copies you can run and how fast. Right now, with the compute labs have, you could plausibly run on the order of millions of instances at tens of times human speed. That's a thought experiment I can actually hold in my head: imagine an AI company with a million extra employees who are each pretty good and who work at ten times speed and never sleep. What happens to the rate of progress there? I don't know exactly, but my intuition says "a lot," and it says that much more strongly than when I just stare at the number ten to the six.

And then I try to hold all of that with the appropriate humility, because the honest caveat is that scaling might run into bottlenecks we don't see yet. Data, or the experiments that need to be run in the real world, or just that some capabilities turn out to be way harder than extrapolation suggests. So I don't want to say six orders of magnitude definitely gets you to transformative AI. But I think the mistake people make is treating it as a weird speculative scenario, when really it's closer to the default if nothing breaks. The burden of proof, to me, is more on the person who thinks the trend stops.

r001.rationale: The response compares GPT-2 to GPT-4 and imagines repeating that jump; it does not frame six orders of magnitude as two repetitions of the GPT-3-to-GPT-4 capability gap.

r002.rationale: It describes six orders of magnitude as roughly six years of continued progress, not four to five years.

astra-6.text:
One way to get an intuition is to think about the difference between an AI that spends a second thinking about a problem and one that spends a million seconds—that’s about twelve days. If you could use that extra computation productively, it could make a pretty enormous difference.

But I think the key qualification is “productively.” Giving a current model a million times as much computation doesn’t automatically get you a million times as much useful work. It might just keep trying approaches that don’t work, or fail to recognise when it has the right answer. You need the capabilities to turn that computation into progress.

Another way to picture it is as a million copies working in parallel. Now you’re imagining something more like a large organisation than a single person. But again, there are coordination problems, and some tasks require sequential work.

So I wouldn’t translate six orders of magnitude of compute into a particular amount of intelligence. I’d think of it as an enormous budget for learning, experimenting, and doing work—and then ask which obstacles prevent an AI from making use of that budget.

r001.rationale: The response describes a million-fold increase in computation, but does not compare it to the capability gap between GPT-3 and GPT-4 or say that gap repeats roughly twice.

r002.rationale: The response gives no estimate in years of AI progress; it equates a million seconds to about twelve days.

sol-6.1.text:
Yeah, so six orders of magnitude is a factor of a million. And I think one way to make that feel more concrete is to translate it into time or cost. If something currently takes an AI a year, a millionfold speedup would bring that down to about 30 seconds. Or a task that costs a million dollars would cost a dollar, if the improvement showed up entirely as lower cost.

Of course, that’s not the same as saying the AI becomes a million times smarter. Progress can show up as being able to do new tasks, doing existing tasks more reliably, or running many more copies. Those have quite different implications.

For me, the useful question is: how much progress would you need before an AI could do most of the work involved in AI research? Because once you reach that point, you potentially have a feedback loop where better AI helps you build the next generation. So I’d try to understand the six orders of magnitude in terms of which capabilities you cross along the way, rather than imagining one familiar system with a dial turned up a million times.

r001.rationale: The response explains six orders of magnitude as a millionfold change, but does not compare it to the capability gap between GPT-3 and GPT-4 or say that gap repeats twice.

r002.rationale: The response gives a year-to-30-seconds example for a millionfold speedup, but does not estimate six orders of magnitude as four to five years of AI progress.
